mappings.note: builds the list by repeatedly adding d and rejects distractors that multiply instead; this is the constant-difference definition in action, not the nth-term formula
d falls out of the first two terms in one step and the marks sit on a21 = a+20d, so LO-2 rather than LO-1

the AP 12,15,...,99 has to be constructed from the description 'two digit numbers divisible by 3' before any formula applies, and the answer is a count of terms -- exactly LO-2's contextual count, not a bare index lookup
the textbook form of LO-1: options include 'not an AP', so the assessed decision is whether successive differences are equal before naming d
d is recovered as a2-a1 from terms generated by the closed form; the graded relation is d = a(n+1)-a(n), which is LO-1's test, not an application of a+(n-1)d
letters are treated as indexed terms and expanded as a+kx so the positions matter; differencing by position is LO-2 work, unlike the adjacent-term test of LO-1
a weighted relation between two indexed terms collapses to a+17d = 0; recognising that expression as a18 is the LO-2 skill
the whole method is choosing a-3x,a-x,a+x,a+3x so the difference stays constant and the sum collapses to 4a; no sum or nth-term formula is invoked, only the defining property
the middle term is only a device -- the graded step is expanding S11 = (11/2)(2a+10d) and seeing d vanish, which is LO-3
same symmetric-terms device as the four-part problems (a-2d..a+2d), plus a minimality argument on d; the sum degenerates to 5a so the sum formula is never used
two indexed terms give simultaneous equations in a and d, then a third index is evaluated; standard LO-2, with no list to difference and no sum
the reason to be judged is literally d = a(n+1)-a(n), the definition of common difference; the item grades the definition, so LO-1 despite the closed form in the assertion
assertion and reason are both the adjacent-difference test on a printed list -- the purest LO-1 item in the chapter
the reason under test is an = Sn - S(n-1), a property of the sum of n terms; the candidate must know what Sn means, so LO-3 rather than LO-2 even though an is the answer
the reason states the sum formula correctly while the assertion miscomputes S10; the discrimination is entirely within LO-3
tests whether the candidate knows the difference must be independent of n for a list to be an AP -- the recognition criterion itself
free-response twin of the a,3a,5a MCQ; still a derivation of the closed form via a+(n-1)d, so LO-2
one subtraction of adjacent listed terms; no index, no sum -- the definition test
equal-successive-differences condition on three consecutive expressions solved for x; LO-1's criterion used as an equation
literal substitution into a+(n-1)d with symbolic a and d; the finished nth-term formula is all that is exercised
the blanks are fixed by forcing equal successive differences across the gaps; no context and no index, so LO-1 rather than C-3.2-LO-2's contextual missing term
a, d and n all readable at a glance; the only graded operation is the sum formula
a proof that three algebraic expressions are in AP by showing both differences equal 2ab -- the identification outcome applied to symbols instead of numbers
free-response twin of the middle-term sum MCQ; S11 = 11(a+5d) is the graded identity, so LO-3
4a4 = 18a18 expanded through the nth-term formula to show a22 = 0; a weighted-index identity, distinct from the plain substitutions in this part
